utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, your first witness today is FWS-73; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, you gave us some homework for the weekend, to verify something. So I don't know if this is a good time or perhaps should I do it later, in relation to the transcript and what you told us to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now we've got the witness in court, I think it might be better to deal with it later, after one of the breaks. The witness's pseudonym document will be Exhibit P430, and it will be under seal. Now, sir, will you please stand up and make the solemn declaration in the document which is being given to you. Are you able to hear the proceedings through your earphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please, and come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. Could you move your chair closer to the microphones and speak up slightly. Would you try again, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you look at the sheet of paper in front of you, you see a number on it. It's number 73. That is your pseudonym in these proceedings. Below this pseudonym there is a name and a nickname. Is it your name and your nickname?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Below the name, there is a date. Is it your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Below your birth date there is the name of a private enterprise. Did you own this enterprise before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the sheet of paper, there are several other names of other protected witnesses. So in your testimony, if you want to refer to these people, please do not tell their name but use their code number. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Two, two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which part of the town did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The old town centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a Muslim neighbourhood or mixed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: It was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you live near the Careva mosque?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, I lived near the Careva mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this mosque destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: That mosque and all the mosques in Foca were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the destroyed mosque after it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When it was -- when the mosque was set on fire, I was at home and then, when they made me do forced work and as we were returning from Brod, I saw it -- or rather, even its foundations had become unrecognisable by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean you saw that while you were detained, the remains?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: While I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you live in a house -- in a house or in an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I lived in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this house destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: That house, first the roof tiles were taken off, then windows and everything that could be taken away was taken away. I watched it as I walked to Brioni to work, three kilometres away, and I could see my house and I could -- every day when I went to work, I could see them remove the roof, the window frames and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The private enterprise that you owned, did Serbs come to your enterprise before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, Serbs did come to that enterprise on various occasions, and they even provoked - teased - us before the war. They fired from the -- from a neighbouring restaurant, from a neighbouring coffee bar, (redacted) (redacted). We reported them to the police before the war, but they could do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How much time before the war; just a few days before or even longer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On the eve of the war or perhaps a month before it broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those who provoked you, who were they? What kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Those who provoked me and the rest of the citizenry were people of orthodox ethnicity who at that time, on the eve of the war, already were out and they were under the instructions of Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those persons that you just mentioned, were they SDS politicians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They were politicians of the SDS, or should I say extremist politicians of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that these people were in charge of those who provoked you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I was born in the town of Foca so that I frequently patronised a fish restaurant which is on the bank of the Drina, and the waiters there were of different ethnic origins, and they told me -- and I would see them with my own eyes when they met at Ribarski, so that all people of Muslim ethnicity had to vacate that place, had to leave when they would meet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "they," do you mean these politicians you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The politicians. These politicians that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not a single one, neither before nor during nor after or now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you involved in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In no way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why then did you become a target? Why was your enterprise targeted with provocations and even shots?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Everybody who owned a business in Foca was the target of these people who -- of the agents provocateurs, of these agents. They wanted to destroy those private businesses with their provocations and to drive us away, everybody who owned a private business.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "everybody," do you mean all owners of enterprises, regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, only Muslim businessmen. They were the target of attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca, did you participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca, I was in my enterprise and it was just to open or, rather, we had just begun work. Then I saw crowds of people coming out, and I thought it was a strike because there had been such occurrences before. So I was at home in my enterprise, unaware of the war or anything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you stay in your home during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I spent nine days at home, in hell, in fear. Nine days later, to my -- Seselj's men, Arkan's men came to my house, and there were all sorts of Chetnik formations. Those were young men from Foca. I knew them all. And they came to my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those young men from Foca, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They were all with weapons, so that I cannot describe it to you now. After all the gunfire, after all the shooting, I thought that was the end of me, my wife, and the woman who worked for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see weapons distributed to young men in Foca or anything related to this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On the eve of the war, just before it broke out, cars brought people, young men, with their car boots full of weapons, and in one enterprise, I saw it, how they took them out publicly without -- in the open. I saw that, but I never thought that something like that would begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did this happen? You mentioned another enterprise. What was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, it happened -- it happened -- I cannot tell you about it now - I believe the Court knows that - where I could see it all with my own eyes from my enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Court does not know what you have said previously. You have to tell the Court now and today. So do you know the name of this enterprise where you saw weapons being unloaded?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw it (redacted). (redacted), and I could see directly how weapons were being taken out and other similar things.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your own enterprise, was it ever looted or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, during the war, while you were in your home.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: During the war, during the war, that same day, all that was in it was looted even by those people who used to work there, and everything was broken down, completely destroyed by those people, I mean, of the Orthodox ethnicity. That same day, everything was broken, destroyed, and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested after nine days. What day, actually, was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When this group of Seselj's men, Arkan's men, as they sat at my place, I had to offer them drinks which I had in my cellar, which was, as a matter of fact, outside beyond that shop, and we sat there for about two or three hours. I asked them if they could let me go, leave Foca, and they said no. Three hours later, they sent two armed men, and my wife and I were thus taken under custody to the concentration camp in Foca. That was around the 17th of April. So it began on the 8th. Nine days later, on the ninth day of the war which they were waging, when they were killing and torching, nine days later I was taken to the camp, my wife and I.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those who arrested you, you spoke about two men. What did they wear? What clothing did they have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They wore civilian clothes, I knew them by sight. And there is a village called Livade near Foca. I did not know their names. One had a long beard. They knew me. I did not know them except by sight a little. And they used foul language, they said, "You want sovereign Bosnia, do you?" And things like that. And we kept silent. We dared not speak out because had we said anything, they would have killed us on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did they tell you why you were arrested, except for these remarks related to the sovereign Bosnia? Did they tell you why?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Before the war, they all distanced themselves from us, and we who were there, we naturally all socialised, Muslims and the orthodox, and they all parted company with us and naturally started provocations as they had been taught by Karadzic: "If need be, there will be no more Muslims." And with a group like Maksimovic, Ostojic and others, went by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I had asked you if these two men who arrested you and took you to the camp, did they tell you why, why they take you and your wife and where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They said -- they did not tell us where they were taking us but they did say, "Muslims" -- and over there they call them balijas. So they said, "Balijas, you will see who we are and what we are." And they took us in an unknown direction. We did not know where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you and your wife were taken to the camp. Do you mean the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Before the war, it was called the KP Dom. It was the penitentiary, reformatory, one of the largest in Yugoslavia perhaps, but this KP Dom had been converted into a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you arrive? At what time of the day did you arrive at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We arrived in the KP Dom where -- on a cloudy day. It looked to me as if it was late afternoon, but it could have been around 2.00 or 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the KP Dom after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: For -- I was there two years and six months, that is from the beginning to the end of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did your wife stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: My wife was there one day, two or maybe three, not more than that, because I was so completely lost that I did not know where I was, let alone my wife. I was scared out of my wits. And there was another woman, a female under 33, and I saw the two of them. They let go my wife, that person stayed behind, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You refer to the witness 33 on your sheet, right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This short period that your wife was in the KP Dom, was she with you in the same room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Same room, same room, or rather we had the same anteroom or what do you call it. There were four or five rooms, but in a set of rooms. They were all one next to the other. There were two larger and two smaller, and we were all there in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the entrance of the KP Dom, who was present?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When we arrived, when they threw us out, those two Chetniks, the warden - that is, we later found out he was the warden of the camp - he was in front of the building, at the entrance, and whether there was one policeman or two policemen, but there was somebody with him. On this side there was this policeman, Cancar; we know that. We remember that. And we said, "What's this?" And they said, "Go in and you'll find out what's that." And they sort of shrugged their shoulders to show, I mean, that's nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned a policeman Cancar. Was that a prison guard or was it a policeman from SUP?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said the warden was there and --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, the prison guard, a prison guard. And I think he was a prison guard in the KP Dom even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that the warden was there, but that you did not know that he was the warden at that time. Who was there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We did not know. We did not know that that was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of the person you saw there that you later found out was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just a moment. I remember that moment when we entered. We were frightened. I still again feel that fear, that I cannot really guess at who was the warden, and I simply wonder at myself, because we were so beaten up, so ill treated, that when I even think of it, I feel like killing myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, as we go through this very slowly, so don't worry. Whom did you see? If you tell us the name of the persons that you saw when you arrived. You have already mentioned Mr. Cancar. Who else did you see that you knew?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I -- Milorad Krnojelac, Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was he when you arrived? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He stood in front of the -- by the entrance with two more perhaps, at the entrance into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing there? Could you see? Was he simply standing there or did he do anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He stood in front of the entrance because, since we knew him from before, we said, "Hello. What is this? Why are they bringing us in?" not knowing what he was. I mean, we knew him but did not know what his role was. And all those who were at the entrance had their roles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you said hello to them and said, "What's going on?" what did he say, if anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He behaved very casually. Butter would not melt in his mouth. But he said, "Nothing. Nothing. You will be interrogated, interviewed for two or three days, and then you will be set free."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you continue talking to him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They immediately pushed us through the gate, through the iron gate of the camp. There was no conversation, just a very short conversation, a fleeting conversation, and we were immediately driven into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Krnojelac was wearing when you saw him at the gate?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I remember he wore civilian clothes. And only this policeman was in his old police uniform that they wore before, and Krnojelac was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers on your arrival at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When we entered the KP Dom, there were soldiers, that is, not professional soldiers but as we called them, riff-raff, brought from neighbouring villages in Serbia and neighbouring places in Montenegro. They wore reservist uniforms and they were right there at the beginning when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you call them riff-raff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Some of those who were there, I mean, of the guards, no matter what instructions they received from the administration, they told us every detail, and they said, "We've asked for reinforcements." They thought that we would resist, that we would fight against them, and they had brought reinforcements. And these told us, those selfsame guards - not all of them but individuals - that they had brought people from prisons, from Serbian prisons in Serbia, so that they could slaughter over here, torch, and that -- so that everything they conquered would become theirs. That was what the local ones had ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these sort of soldiers, how long did they stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, what I've been telling you, as far as dates is concerned, is not very accurate. My memory is very poor, especially has been since I left camp. But perhaps a month, something around a month. I really don't know. They weren't there very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say your memory is very poor, you mean in relation to dates?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Dates, dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Krnojelac was at the entrance. Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did know him before the war because Foca is not really a very big town. So all of us who live there knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I knew where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever go to this house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I personally did not visit him at home, but I came to his cafe, rather, the cafe that was opened by his son. So I stopped by there, say around two or three times, before the war, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know which of Krnojelac -- who of Krnojelac's sons was running the cafe? Do you know his name and who he was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The names? No, I don't know his sons' names. They are young people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krnojelac involved in politics before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Everybody from Foca, from street cleaners to professors, doctors, judges, everybody was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually see Mr. Krnojelac on SDS functions, rallies, meetings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention. When they went to Ribarski, that's where they held their meetings. However, as soon as he took the job of warden of the KP Dom, he was with them non-stop. Perhaps some of them did this surreptitiously whereas others did it publicly before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does it mean that it's your conclusion that Mr. Krnojelac was in the SDS because he got this function in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Only if he had been a member of the SDS could he have become a person to hold that position and other similar monster-like positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krnojelac have a function in the reserve army? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I found out that he was a Captain before the war, a reserve Captain, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There were reserves, so there would be this reserve of a week, ten days, a month, and after that reserve, even those who had a bit more rank would not even take off their uniforms. So then you could see who was who because there were quite a few of them, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Krnojelac wearing uniforms at these exercises that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. Saw him after these exercises, promenading through town in this uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any ranks on the uniform, or how do you know that he was a Captain?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw those little stars, you know, at that time. There were three or four stars and that meant Captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you see him in this uniform? Can you estimate how much prior to the war that was, that you saw him last?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: A lot, a lot before the war, because just before the war, the reserves were over and everything else was over. I can't remember the dates exactly. Just before the war, there were no such exercises, you see. I mean these reserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said when you saw him at the KP Dom, you did not know that he was the warden. When did you learn that he was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When these military extremists left the KP Dom, then people knew who the warden was and everything else, because all of these people who worked there from the very outset, in spite of what they were told, that is that they would be killed as well if they talked to us about anything, if they discussed anything with us, but I can say that there were some people who told us everything, at the very outset, who was what in the KP Dom, in the camp, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And did -- who told you that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: If I had the numbers here -- I mean, this is pretty difficult for me because there are still extremists over there until the present day and although everything is protected around here, I wouldn't like to give any names, the names of these persons, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The best thing would be -- if they are not on the list already, is to let him write them down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can the witness have a sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Those two, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are not witnesses and they have no witness numbers. These are actually two staff members of the KP Dom. We should maybe assign --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are they referred to in that document we have? I have forgotten the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They can be referred to there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. A second, please. While my colleague is finding out the number, I think I can continue, or shall we first get this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, we will show you the document in a moment once they have got the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is precisely what I wished to say, that the Defence is very curious. We would really like to have a good look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We just add the numbers and then I will hand this over. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those you just wrote down, did they actually talk with you and mention that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They talked to me and what they said was who were all the people who meant anything over there. To them, I mean. They didn't mean a thing to us, but they said to us the following: "Such and such a person is the main person there and this other one is his assistant." They told us everything. I mean, well, that's what they told me. That's what they told me personally. But I don't know if they told other people about this as well. So from the very beginning, I knew who was who over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you said that one was the -- one was the main person and there was one -- one was the assistant, who was the main person and who was the assistant? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The warden of the KP Dom, of this camp, was Milorad Krnojelac, and the deputy was Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I would just like to give back this piece of paper to you in case you know the first name of the second person. Do you know the first name, then? You would have to add it. Or do you know just simply the nickname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would be best still to have it written down, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If the document can be handed back to the witness, he can have a look at it. If he can give us any further identification of that particular person, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The two persons are on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, can we have a reference in the transcript to their numbers in that particular exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I've given it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought that is what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was doing. I'm sorry, could you give it back to counsel, please? Just give it back to counsel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The numbers are already on the paper, so I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's just have them recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The first name is 119 from the list and the other name is 102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what is the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. This document will be marked Exhibit P431, and it will be under seal. You've seen this document, have you, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These two persons whose names you have written down, did they talk to you only once about the position of Mr. Krnojelac and Mr. Todovic, or on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This was on several occasions. Not only them but the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean, "Not only them but the others"? Do you mean additional prison staff members spoke about that to you as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There were. There were other members too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did a brother of Mr. Krnojelac work in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He did work at the KP Dom. He was a driver. On one occasion, he drove us to his village, the village of Zavajt. We were loading wood at that time, so I saw him. He personally drove us there. Also before that, he was a driver too while this was really a KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say, "He drove us," who else was -- which other detainee was with you? If it is someone from the list, please say the number.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Number 77 is one of them, was there too, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you talk with the brother about Mr. Krnojelac, about Mr. Milorad Krnojelac, or did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When we had set out for that village of Zavajt, we went to a man who made barrels. We loaded a barrel on, onto the truck, and then he unloaded it in front of his house. There was a man from that village there too. He talked to him, and he said, "I told my brother not to take that duty." We heard that with our very own ears. It was strange to us. They were still killing and torching, and we were wondering why he was saying all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you heard the brother of Milorad Krnojelac talk about Milorad in this way to this neighbour, where were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We were there, three or four metres away. We had unloaded this barrel, and we were waiting to board the truck again because we had to drive for an additional kilometre or so to the place where we were supposed to load the wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you're not remembering dates very well. Can you tell us when this was, approximately? Was it after the replacement of Mr. Krnojelac or during his time as the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: While he was still warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can you say which year this happened, that you heard that, or maybe the season?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The season might have been the month of July or August, whatever. As for all of these things that we did, when we were allowed to go out and do that, well, it could have been a year or two that had elapsed, something like that. Perhaps a year or two after the war had started. I can't remember whether it was autumn or summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But you had already been quite some time in the KP Dom; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who was supervising Mr. Krnojelac and the prison staff from outside? Who was above them -- who gave them the orders? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: All the orders that they received, they received from these extremist groups led by Maksimovic and Ostojic. However, however, they pretended, when they were talking to us, that it was some third party telling them what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who spoke about a third party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There were some of our people from the camp who were beseeching them to let them go out because they had lost such a lot of weight, and they were sick, and they were asking to be released in every possible way because they had done nothing wrong. They had done nothing as such. Their only mistake had been that they were Muslims. And the answer they invariably got was that now it is not these local people who are in charge, that there is some kind of third party who came to run the show. So it's not that there were these local people who were in charge, but even when the local people were in charge, there was killing and there was destruction of property, et cetera, et cetera. So actually, they were deceiving them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that Ostojic, Maksimovic, they were giving orders. How do you know that? Is that your conclusion from their position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: All of Foca saw, on the eve of the war, Ostojic, Maksimovic, Cancar when they met, when they were calling upon the Serb population to join them, to rally together. This was public. We all saw them. There was not a single person from that town who had not seen that. Also we knew while I was at home, until I was taken prisoner, that is, Chetnik soldiers said -- when they started torching and when they started killing, they were giving the names of the persons who had ordered them to do what they were doing. That is to say, those same names of persons who we saw meeting in Foca. And they even stood guard all night so that nobody would attack them, although there was no war there from the Muslim side. They said the names of the persons whom they were guarding. They did not conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were talking about the time before the war. Did you ever see any of these politicians you just referred to? Did you ever see them in the prison, in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw Maksimovic. There was this working part of the KP Dom that functioned as a furniture factory, and now the previous convicts who had not finished making this furniture left some of that furniture behind. So then our people who were detained in the camp were told to finish this furniture. Maksimovic came and he took away some of that furniture. Of course, he was with the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him actually with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I worked at all the places, from the easiest to the hardest one. At that time, I was chopping wood, and that was five metres from the factory, inside, in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] -- they pass you, Mr. Maksimovic, and --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We usually tried to get out of the way, to avoid attracting their attention to -- we tried to hide, not to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, let us return a little bit in time to the beginning of your detention. When you came into the KP Dom, were you mistreated or abused, either on the way to the KP Dom or at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On the way to the KP Dom, I was so frightened, I was so afraid of those young men, that I thought they would slaughter us, because when I saw and heard torching, gunfire, we thought that was the end. And they ill-treated us so badly that we kept wondering, what's all this? What's it? And when I arrived in the KP Dom, those who, as they called themselves, soldiers - and we know they are killers and thieves from Serbian and Montenegrin prison - they, on the orders of the local Chetniks, took out young men to a hallway. If you open the door, there is the hallway where we are and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you here. We are coming to these beatings and mistreatment within the camp just a few minutes later. You said that you were ill-treated on the way to the KP Dom. In which way? Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: As we went, with their hands and feet and, "Balijas, what do you want?" and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you searched when you entered the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Searched from A to Z, as the saying goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you registered? Were your particulars taken down?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They took down our names. I think Cancar was the one who did it, policeman Cancar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken within the KP Dom? Into which building and into which room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When we arrived in the KP Dom, there was a room in the first building on the ground floor, and when we got there, they put us there, and we saw there beaten people. We could barely recognise them. It was a Croat. I think he was a TV mechanic. Another one was -- worked in a shop. I could not recognise them. And there were sobs and crying. At first, we were all put there, and I heard that allegedly the camp had been opened that day and as they would bring people from their homes, they would put them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the number of the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Believe me, numbers and dates, because I know it was the first building, the first building as you enter, and the ground floor. I mean, it is slightly above the ground, there are some stairs there where they brought us, but it is the ground floor where they brought us, a room on the ground floor. There were several rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness Exhibit 18, the photo 7512. It's this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the photo, and if it is possible, point out the room where you were taken in. You said a building 1, and can you --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This here room, this one here. That's it. That's the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour, is pointing at --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: As you walk up these stairs and turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The witness was pointing at the building 1, ground floor, the room to the left side, this left wing. And I think we can say it's Room 11. I think there is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I cannot be absolutely sure about dates or so, but I'd say it was less than a month. We, four of us, were immediately transferred to the kitchen and those other people stayed there and we were isolated in that other building, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many detainees were together with you in this first room, approximately? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the first room, it wasn't only one room. It was several rooms, but the same passage and the same entrance. So that by day and by night, more and more people were getting in. It was overcrowded. When I was there, it was simply overcrowded. It was absolutely overfilled with people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, you're letting your voice drop every now and again, and the interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. Could you pull the microphone more directly towards you and lean slightly forward?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Sorry. I am sorry. Sorry. Do you want me to repeat what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think they have heard you, thank you, this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have not yet mentioned how many -- you said a lot of people were there and it became more and more. What was the highest number of detainees in this room, in this set of rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, would it be 70, 80, I don't know, because I did not count them. And new people kept coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you mentioned that you were -- after some time, you were taken into the other building, in the building number 2, into which room, on which floor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Ground floor again, ground floor again. I think, yes, the first storey.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And do we still have the photo there? Yes. Would you point this room out on the photo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness pointed out the ground floor, the ground floor of this wing number 2, and I think we can be -- we can say that it is Room 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 16 or in this other -- in this second room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not very long either, because near us there could have been several Serbs who were prisoners in the KP Dom and for some reason or other had not left. And those men did not want them to talk to us or communicate with us or something, so that we didn't spend much time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So that means you were transferred to other rooms as well within the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, again inside, because after awhile, more people were detained and the rooms downstairs would simply be too crowded. There would be one over the other. So they began to put people in other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The detainees that you met in the first room and other rooms, were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Down to the last one. Civilians, all of them. They were all brought from their homes. Now, of course, I cannot vouch for those who arrived from the vicinity, but those who were from the town, I can vouch for them, and there were quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In the initial period of your detention in the first room you were in, was anyone called out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In this room where we were in the beginning, they called out -- called a last name Cedic, last name Isanovic. And in the hallway, which was a metre away from the door that you used to go into our rooms, they would batter those young men. What does it mean, "batter"? Beat them up fiercely so that they screamed. And we were so silent that you could hear a fly there. Then they would be brought back into our room again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took them out of the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On the orders of local Chetniks. The forces that had come for them, those murderers and thieves, they killed them -- I mean, beat them. But the orders came from our local ones because they did not know who is this and who is that one. It was as those others told them, that they took them out and beat the daylights out of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's stick to what you actually saw and heard. These soldiers who called the two men out, did they call their names? Did they call them out by name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Last name. Last name, surname. We were so many that they didn't have the slightest who is who and what is whose name. They would call out. They would say, "Who is this one? Who is that?" And he would, of course, say, "I'm the one. That's me." Last names.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was any guard, a normal prison guard, with them on these occasions when they called out these two men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Always. Always, invariably, because he is the one who brings the order for ill-treatment, for battery and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said they were taken into a room or a corridor or hall. Where? Next to the room where you were or where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Right there by the entrance. There is a small anteroom, and into the entrance into our rooms there is an anteroom. Like this door here. Right behind it is a door and that is the anteroom, before the entrance, the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did you hear? What did you hear when they were taken there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We heard they immediately began to beat them, and those young men began to scream and wail. After awhile, they brought those same young men back into those same rooms where we were and they were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on them, and if so, what kind of injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Only a short time later, they were all swollen. We could see bruises, but after some time, we could see how their faces were swollen. And we asked, "Where?" and they said, "All over," but faces you could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the witness was telling, he was pointing at his face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said one of them was a certain Isanovic. Do you know his name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: One was Isanovic. And there was another Isanovic who had been brought beaten up, and he was near our room, separately. Names I don't know because they're quite young. I know their surnames, I know them by sight, but they were much younger than I so that I don't know their names, only their surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a Kemo Isanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Kemo. You're right. That's it. Kemal Isanovic. Yes, his name is Kemal Isanovic, and he was beaten up alongside this Cedic. Yes, Kemo, Kemal. Okay. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person Kemo Isanovic is on Schedule B, number 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said he was a young man. Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He's from a locality called the Cohodor Mahala, which is part of Foca. A young man, a very young man, a lad.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "a very young man, a lad," what do you mean? Around how old was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He could have been not more than 25, I don't think. Twenty-seven, 22. I can't say really. Well, which is relatively young.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this person Cedic, can you tell us anything about him? How old was he? Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He was also from Cohodar Mahala, from the same locality as Isanovic. He looked even younger to me, younger than Isanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Zaim Cedic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know a Cedic. He was a lawyer at Tjentiste. He also arrived all beaten up. We asked him how, where? He said, "They beat me non-stop, then non-stop they forced me to eat salt." "I ate pounds of salt," he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This lawyer Cedic, that is not the Cedic you meant? This is not the young man you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, no, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What became of these two young men? Did they survive the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Those two young men were beaten and then taken away and killed. And you will wonder how is it that we know that they were killed. Because everything that went on inside and outside we learned from those men of ours. I can say "our men," because had all the Chetniks been the same, we'd all have disappeared. And through this Court, I can, if anybody asks my opinion to mention them openly, but the time has not come yet to mention them because there are still extremist groups on the ground there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean you got this information from prison staff or other Serbs outside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Naturally. Off the staff, off the prison staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said these two young men, this Cedic and Isanovic, they were beaten up and killed. Does that mean they were taken out again and beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Again, again. And when those extremists from Montenegro and Serbia had left, they continued to beat them and take them away so that they are missing. They were taken away several times more. But I could not see that because, at that time, I had already left that room. But I heard it from other people, from other people who were in those rooms, and it is 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also mentioned another Isanovic. Who was that and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This Isanovic had a coffee shop where I saw, and as much as I told, perhaps it was one of the best coffee shops in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after the war had broken out, those same who had come to my room, when they came, they said, "We are sorry," presumably. They always said, "We are sorry." I say made as if they were sorry. And, "We are sorry but we set this place of his on fire." And one of those Seselj's men said, "Well, I've been there with my girlfriend a hundred times or more and I'm really sorry that we had to torch it." And this Adnan Isanovic was beaten up, he bled, and he was in the room next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he taken out of the KP Dom in this initial period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the initial period, he was taken away as if to have him examined in the hospital, which is beyond comprehension because they are killing, they are torching, and we couldn't understand how is it that they take our man to have him examined by a doctor. And later on we learned that Adnan Isanovic, one Selimovic, who had his car repair shop, and another one whose name I cannot remember, that they were all taken out by the hospital and killed. And we were also immediately told that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who told you? And how did you --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: All the staff of the camp. That is, there were several men who -- whom I've mentioned, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also hear about their fate on radio?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, thanks for reminding me. A journalist, Semso Tucakovic, had. I can say certain things in public. A woman of Serb ethnicity who told him about everything that went on in and around the camp, so that these extremist groups thought that Semso Tucakovic was in Foca, and they searched all the cellars and basements and everything again because he reported the truth and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. We just want to stick to certain victims that you mentioned and that you saw, and just finish these -- the questions related to them. Did you hear on radio that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, we also heard it on the radio. But that information, we hear the same thing within an hour in the camp, and also on the radio, the transistors which we hid very well because they were not accessible to us, and we listened on them -- we listened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were also Serbs in the KP Dom. Where were they kept? Were they always kept separate from the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Later on, a few months later, they began to detain Serbs. They were in the next building, in the adjacent building, in this other building, on an upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who were they? Why were they in the KP Dom? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Serbs detained in the KP Dom. There was one among them, and I'm 100 per cent sure that he refused to join that Chetnik formation. And others, when the spoils are split up, when they loot, when they rob, when they pillage, and then when distributing their booty, they cannot decide who will get -- who will take what and they simply pull out their pistols and their automatic weapons and kill each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those Serb detainees that you saw there, how were they dressed? Were they civilians? Were they soldiers? What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Some of them came in those many-coloured uniforms and some wore Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this one person that you said you knew and you were sure that he did, he refused to join formations, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: If -- shall I write his name, please, on a paper? I'd rather not pronounce it loudly because, I repeat, there are still extremists down there who had not been caught. So that until one experiences it, one cannot simply grasp what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, if there is no problem with that, can the witness have a sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it might be better if you dealt with that during the short adjournment, by finding out whether it's on the list of the other exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's not. It's a Serb citizen. And it can be shown to the Defence counsel, and the only question I have in relation to this and then we should have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person, did he personally tell you that he refused to join the army?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No. He did not tell that to me personally. I was told by detainees in the camp who came from the same institution that he had worked in, and they went to mow grass. And all the Chetniks who were there spoke about that person, that he was ready to clean all of the loos or anything but that he would not take up arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That document will be Exhibit P432, and it will be under seal. We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you have to work in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In prison, you had to work. Whenever orders came in, no questions were put. You had to do whatever these orders said you had to do. Anything, anything, anything that you were ordered to do, you had to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who ordered you to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Orders were transferred by Savo Todovic. If Savo Todovic was not present, then he would order these guards, and we had to even call them officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Savo Todovic personally give you some tasks? Did he personally call you out for certain labour?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He got orders from the administration, and he transferred those orders to us over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question was: Did he personally give you tasks? Did he personally speak to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, he did personally, and the guards did. They had lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you start to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not even a month had gone by before I started working, on orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you have to do first? Can you give us the tasks in order, in the way -- chronological order?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: At first, I worked in the kitchen. I worked there for a few months. When I watched the prisoners who were the same as I was, when I saw them fainting from hunger, I tried to give them a little piece of bread on the sly so that nobody could see, guards and the kitchen staff. When they saw what I was doing, then I got expelled from the kitchen. Afterwards they called me back into the kitchen. The same thing happened again because I could not take it. I was in the same position as they were, and I could not watch my fellow citizens fainting from hunger. Then I was expelled again. After that, I was forced to do all kinds of jobs that had to be done within and outside the KP Dom. That included chopping wood, also felling trees and loading wood. And they said that this was for their veterans. And the Chetniks who killed the most and slaughtered the most were called veterans by them, and we had to provide wood for them. After loading wood, then I had to go and cut grass for hay. However, since I didn't know how to cut grass for hay, at least I could load it if nothing else. After that loading, we also worked up there at the farm which was within the KP Dom before. We were also digging, doing lots of agricultural work. We were cleaning kitchen coops, pigsties, et cetera. We were digging holes for the swine that perished and things like that. So I was forced to do all these different kinds of jobs. When I last worked at the central workshop, I could not take it any more. On orders, somebody's orders, Savo Todovic was forcing me to work all the time and things like that. So those were the jobs that I did while in the camp. One of the jobs also was when they forced four of us to dig a grave for this mechanic who was an ethnic Muslim. This was at a later stage. All kinds of jobs. As I said, we did all sorts of things. I had all these different jobs. And there were many things that had to be done, and whatever had to be done, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever dare to refuse to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, if you would dare to refuse -- I dared once and I know that immediately they would beat you, throw you into an isolation cell and then no one knew how you would end.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this actually happen to you when you refused to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I refused to work, and then Savo Todovic came to the room where I was and then he kicked me all the way to work, and he was cursing my balija mother and saying all sorts of things he shouldn't have said. And maybe I could even be his father, in terms of age, but that's the way he treated me. That's what happened. So, no way, theoretically even, you could not refuse anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you paid for your work in any way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Oh, come on. No way. You couldn't even think of any pay. I don't know how to express myself really. We were Muslims whom they had underestimated to such an extent that they killed them, they beat them. There was no law that was in force. Nothing. We could not discuss pay even theoretically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get extra food when you worked?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, I worked -- I mean, I was in the kitchen when extra food was given. That was a small extra slice and some water. So, for example, if we wouldn't get that, the next day we couldn't move. I mean, to do that same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have listed the various works you did, especially the farm jobs and the agricultural jobs. Was it hard work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Among all these different jobs that I was forced to do, I was also forced to work in the mine. I didn't tell you about the mine. These were jobs that were hard, even for people who were free men, let alone for us malnourished prisoners. And I forgot to mention that we also unloaded flour for the bakery. When we would pick up a sack of flour, we would fall. However, you'd have to do everything. They would say, "Well, you will get a bit of bread," and we broke our backs. We were falling. Some people literally fell. I fell too because the sack of flour was so heavy. And can you imagine working in a mine? In the mine in Miljevina, when they took us there, that's a mine that's not even protected or anything. I don't know how they worked in that mine before the war too. So that was death, death. It was death to go and do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever work on the house of the accused Krnojelac or the cafe in the house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I worked in the cafe of Mr. Krnojelac with another young man who was a plumber. After the cafe, I also worked in a shop, Krnojelac's shop. The cafe was Krnojelac's while this shop had actually belonged to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's first stick with the cafe. How often did you have to work in the cafe and what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the cafe, I was with this plumber, and we were doing things with water pipes. He wanted the water to be in another place as compared to where it had been before that. I don't know. We were there for about two or three days. However, we were doing that when the warden had already been replaced. That's when we were doing that particular job. I mean the warden of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you were -- when you went to this cafe, who took you there and how?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We were personally taken by Warden Krnojelac in his car.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was -- were you guarded while you were doing the work? Were there additional guards there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There was no one there. There were no guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said there was a plumber with you. Who was that? If the person is on the list, just say the number. Otherwise you can say the name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Hajric is his last name. His last name. And his nickname is Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was a detainee in the KP Dom as well as you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, also a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you had to work in a shop. Whose shop was it before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: That shop was Saja Sahinpasic's. He had bought it just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who took you there for doing work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Also the warden, the previous warden. By then there was already a new warden, but then it was the former warden. I don't know how he was replaced and what happened, but at any rate, he took us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did you work in this shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, we worked there for about an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This shop, you said that it was of Mr. Sahinpasic, from before the war. Who is now the owner of the shop? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. During the war, all privately-owned businesses were taken by extremists, as we call them, those who made a name for themselves by torching, killing, and slaughtering. So all private businessmen who had shops, all of them were killed. I personally heard the Serb radio when we were working up there at Brioni. Brioni is three kilometres away from Foca. And that belonged to that previous KP Dom and now it was taken over by the camp. And we were listening to the radio that such-and-such business premises were up for rent, and they would be rented by the veterans, as they call them, and then these veterans, who had made a name for themselves by killing and looting and slaughtering, would take them over, and that is well known in Foca until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took over Sahinpasic's shop; Mr. Krnojelac himself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an absolutely leading question. "Who took over the shop? Did Krnojelac personally do it?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It certainly looks like it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Is there some previous evidence of that fact, that he had taken it over?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't think that he did. I only asked the witness because he said, "He took me there."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Therefore, I would like to know, do you know who actually took over Sahinpasic's shop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've rather destroyed the value of any answer by asking the question, I hasten to add, but the objection is upheld. You can ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who took over this shop, Sahinpasic's shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This is what I have to say: Sahinpasic's shop was taken over by Warden Krnojelac, who handed that shop over to his son. There is proof of that. There was proof of that then, and there is proof of that until this present day. I don't see anything in that that cannot be understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the son of Mr. Krnojelac present when you did your task there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He was present, both in the cafe and in the shop. And it was said that since Krnojelac's son fought at the front line and stepped on a mine - there was no fighting there or anything like that - and both his limbs were blown away; since he had other sons, he decided to give this shop to this son and he would be working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were working there, you said Krnojelac's son was present. Was he handicapped at that time when you worked there, and if so, what did you see? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. He -- he had no legs, in the cafe, and then -- had no legs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Did the son who had lost his legs take over the cafe or the shop or both?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He took over the shop. Warden Krnojelac has other sons. He told me that one would work at the cafe, whereas this other one who had lost his legs would work in the shop, that he would sort of supervise things and that his wife would actually be working and that he would look after it as if it were his own shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which son took over the cafe? Would you know who?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The name? I don't know the name of either one of them. I just know their last names because they are his sons. I was with them, both sons, and one of the sons actually drove me when we were -- drove us, rather, when we were supposed to go for an exchange, and then he said that he was the son. I mean, he was on the bus, sort of escorting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you -- where did you work first, in the cafe or in the shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: At first we worked at the cafe, and then when we finished at the cafe, then they told us that they had some little things that had to be done at the shop. So after the cafe, we went to the shop to take care of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, this son who had no legs was always there too. He was always there. He would sit there, and he was supervising us, watching what we were doing. Although these others came every now and then, he spent more time with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who else was present besides the son who had lost his legs? Was Mr. Krnojelac present?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you talk to each other? I mean, you and Mr. Krnojelac, did you talk?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I talked -- well, here is one subject. I'll describe it very briefly. You know Hajric -- I mean, Krnojelac actually treated me to a brandy too. His son was sitting opposite us, and this Hajric, this Hajric had really had it, both mentally and physically. And I kept telling him, wherever we went to work, "Please don't say anything, because they might kill us." Hajric said he wouldn't talk. Then all of a sudden, he jumped up and he pointed at Krnojelac's son and he said, "Was this necessary?" And I thought that his son would immediately take a gun and kill all of us there. However, we were lucky. So we talked, sort of said, "What is this?" But Krnojelac said, "This will come to an end as well." But all of these were just stories, just stories, whatever was said in the KP Dom. These were false stories. That's what I'm trying to say. When we saw how many people had lost their lives and everything, there was no story that we would believe, that it was not about here or there or wherever. And that proved to be the truth as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I did not really understand what you were referring to. Did you talk about -- with Mr. Krnojelac, about the war? Or did this other, this plumber, refer to the war when he said what -- "Was this necessary?" Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The plumber did not say, "Was this necessary?" He pointed to his son. He said, "Was this necessary?" He didn't use the plural. Like, "What did we need all of this for?" It was sort of like, "Was this necessary, this?"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But what is "this"? I mean, what did he refer to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: "Why was this necessary?" What he meant was that a young man had lost both legs and these young men, under the leadership of these older men, were forced to torch and kill. That is what was meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And how did Mr. Krnojelac behave towards you? How did he treat you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Krnojelac, how he treated me, well, what he did seemed so kind, and it would mean kindness if hundreds and hundreds of beaten and killed persons had not been in that camp. Those who did the beatings were also so kind when you would be with them, and then hundreds and hundreds of our men went missing. I mean, have I explained this sufficiently to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he in any way refer to what had happened in the KP Dom or to the fate of the Muslims? Did he apologise, for instance? Did you speak about it in any way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: None of them talked about that, those who were in the group with Maksimovic and Ostojic. What else do I want to say? Those who were obedient and those who obeyed orders, they --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, just answer my questions, because we come to these other things later on. When -- this son that lost his legs, did you ever see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him. He came to the KP Dom when he had both legs. He had an automatic rifle. He behaved so badly, as if he were conquering the world. He was so haughty. No one dared go out. I don't know what he would have done with any person if he came across him. I worked in the kitchen, you see. Well, he'd never speak to you or something like that, say anything. Not even say hello or anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He came to the KP Dom to visit his father. He was the warden of the KP Dom and, also, he wanted to show how high and mighty he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: As if he were, I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you don't know what exact function he had in the KP Dom, if any?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the KP Dom, no, he did not have any post in the KP Dom, but he did outside the KP Dom, because he was with all those extremist groups. And even outside the KP Dom, when the Chetniks such as Arkan's or others, I don't know, Seselj's men, they said that they went around neighbouring villages, and whatever, old men or a child, they found in these buildings and they would set them on fire. And they were in all those groups. One cannot say. Whoever took up arms, he was with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
