utterances.text: Witness, I simply asked you what his role was in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was he wounded, do you know that, and how he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We heard. When he and perhaps two or three others, when they went up to Tjentiste and in that truck, they came over a mine. And the news spread immediately. Everything that happened outside, we learned about it within a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you learn such news from outside? Who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I've pointed out several times, everything that happened outside we heard it on the transistor radio, but we did not have radios any more. They were abolished and seized and so on. But the staff who worked - now I say "staff" because I can't say about those staff, that they were staff indeed. They were the ones who told us that this has happened, that has happened. Whether to me or to somebody else, I don't know, but I knew about it in any case, and I transmitted it all. I never hid it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the -- the persons Saban Karup and Muharem Alikadic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Alikadic. I know both of them personally, Saban Karup and Muharem Alikadic. One of them, that is Saban, drove a truck for a company and that one was a hauler in his own right. They took them away to be as the vanguard. Chetniks followed them and they were in the trucks in front of them, so that if there was a mine somewhere, or something like that, they would perish and those others would then not take the same road. And after completing that job, they were put in isolation cells so, at that moment, he could not tell us anything about where they'd been, why they'd been there or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Wait for my questions, please. So these two persons were detained in the KP Dom. Were they always kept separate from the -- from you, the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, not always. They were kept for a while, and they would be released. They did not stay non-stop as they thought that it would be a secret. They were also released into rooms. And one of them worked, made the furniture. The other one did the kitchen or the bakery or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you -- did you meet them in the rooms and did you learn from them that they had to drive in front of Serbs? Or how do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: From them, from them personally, is how I learned. From them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually accompany them once on their drives?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I went personally to Slatina which is a village near Foca, to bring in hay for the farm, hay for the livestock. It was cold and so on. And our truck for the first time entered Slatina and that truck was driven by Saban. And we were detainees, like Saban, in the truck, and we were followed by Serb Chetniks. After we passed through, we learned why we were going first. We learned at that very same moment, because we realised, as soon as we were alone and had no escort with us, we realised that we were to drive in front of them. So on that one occasion I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I cannot say. I was there for two months and six months, but that was the first time I entered that village. I cannot really, no. I know it was quite cold, and we went to fetch that hay for the livestock up there at Brioni.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you afraid while you were driven in this first vehicle in front of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Of course we were frightened. But you know, as we rode -- and after that I was frightened. At that particular moment, I really did not care. Death or anything, I was not afraid at that moment. I thought, Well, if I get killed, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This driver, Saban, was it for him the first drive of that sort or had he already done that before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I think he did it before, but I don't really know whether before he went to the isolation cell or afterwards. I think it was after the isolation cell that he undertook another such ride. I think it was after that. Because he was a driver. There was one or two. There was nobody else who could drive it. There was this Muharem and perhaps -- well, and that's it. I don't know if there was another professional driver around.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What became of these two drivers that you just mentioned? Did they survive the camp?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Both drivers survived the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the kitchen. Did you ever see Mr. Krnojelac in the kitchen or in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him in the beginning. I wish to mention, in the beginning, the way he behaved, I thought, This is all great. I shall be out soon. But as the time passed by, six months later I saw him -- it was the first time the Red Cross was allowed to come to Foca, because they would not allow them to put their foot there. So six months later, when the Red Cross came and when they saw people, how emaciated they were, and the Red Cross interpreters were Serbs, and even they could not -- but they were not from Foca. They could not see how people had lost weight, how emaciated they were. So that we asked the Red Cross to improve the quality of food. And I was in the kitchen when Krnojelac, with an interpreter and people from the Red Cross, that is, interpreters were saying to improve food, and then he said, "No way," because he has instructions with those others such as Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar, more torture, more -- so that people fall down from food, and people did fall down and die and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's stay focused on what you heard the ICRC representatives say and Mr. Krnojelac say. What did the ICRC representative ask? What did they say to Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They requested, through the interpreter in the kitchen, and I heard it with my own ears, that they should send, I heard -- and I also heard they had indeed sent food, but it never reached us. And Krnojelac said, "No. We're not going to do that." I think that Rasevic was -- the guard commander was there too. I think he was present. And I heard repeatedly Rasevic and Krnojelac, that they were not to waver for a single moment, that they were not to step away from the plan they had drawn, that is, suffering is there and suffering will remain. So the Red Cross could do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I want to hear from you what exactly Mr. Krnojelac said. You said, "No way. We don't do it." Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He said, "We are not going to do it," and he said it sort of angrily, and that it was out of the question to improve anything, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he say why he could not improve the food? Did --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No. No, not in front of them, because he did not think that they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were -- they wouldn't let them in. They meant nothing to him. Not to him, to this whole extremist part of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, how far were you away from the ICRC and to Mr. Krnojelac when he was having this discussion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Two metres. Not more than that. I cannot give -- tell you to a centimetre, but I heard it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was no food available?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me tell you about food. The quantity of food was such --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. We have already had a lot of witnesses who have told us how the food was. The only question -- so it's not necessary to repeat this. The question is: Was no food available or were your rations kept deliberately so small? That they were small, there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I wonder what the value of that is, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. How can he tell what was in the minds of those who were providing the food? It's a matter of inference, isn't it, that if somebody else got more food than the Muslim detainees, then it was probably deliberate. But nevertheless, I don't think you can ask him to look into the minds of what the people -- the minds of the people who were supplying the food unless they said something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll ask it differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was more food -- was other food available in the prison that you, the detainees, did not get? Did you see anything to this effect?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I put it like this: I understood the question and began answering it. Food that was supplied to the KP Dom, to the camp, was minimal, whilst a cow or anything, so much Muslim livestock, Muslim flour had been plundered that it was overflowing. It was overflowing. But later on, economics set in and they said, "Here. We've got economics." But even in the beginning, when there was surplus food, these people were left to starve, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you beaten while you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the KP Dom, Savo Todovic personally, when he came out or, rather, when he escaped from the prison -- what Ekrem Zekovic escaped from the prison - I think that was his last name - at that time I was responsible for the room, that is, I took care about the hygiene and things like that. I mean, it did not mean anything to them, but I was responsible for the hygiene. So they took out the most suspects from that central workshop where they worked, and some others, and I was one of them. And when they brought me downstairs to a passageway, the same as in the first building, they beat me so badly - and one of the worst beaters was Savo Todovic - so that I urinated blood for a year, for a full year. And they did not beat me with some irons from something, but they had brass knuckles down to the boots. And after that, they put me into an isolation cell, and I spent 12 days there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which building were you when this incident happened, in the building 1 or the building 2?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When it happened, when the incident happened, we were in building number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on which floor were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: First floor, I think. I think first floor. Yes. There is one storey and then the next one. We could even call it the second floor if you count the ground floor as the first floor, that is, the first floor above the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Zekovic, was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic was also in the room, because we were upstairs, and upstairs there was also several rooms. We called it "in the room," because we all communicated. There was one entrance door, and the rest of us were there and it was open.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took you to the place where you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: A guard came. I can't remember his name. He told me to go downstairs because they had to ask me something, and they proceeded to beat me straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where exactly were you beaten; in the same building, in the building number 1, or were you taken to another building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: In the building number 1, ground floor, in the passageway. And they beat there all the others. It just so happened that is where they beat everybody who came, downstairs in that anteroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo 7481 and 7482. Your Honours, for your reference, we are talking now about the incident 5.21 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, if you would look at the bottom photo first, the bottom photo first. Do you know what is shown on the photo? What is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On this -- this photograph shows the staircase. Downstairs is the ground floor, and then you take the stairs to get to our rooms. To the left is also another room, but it was not used. It was used in the beginning. And this is the passageway where they took me. Right behind this is a door. And they just stood in a circle. One hit you from this side, another one from the other side, and so on. So this is the passageway. This is the passage where they beat me and I had come downstairs from the upper floor. And here is a door. This door is locked. In this room there was nobody. I'm sure about that. And here there were the WCs. And that is how they beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the space in front and on the right-hand side, coming down the staircase. Yes, thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Todovic beat you. How did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Those had the brass knuckles and hit me with that, and they would go from one set to the side to the other. When I fell down, when I lost all strength, then they hit me as I was lying down, mostly around head or the lower back, but it was with boots. And he wore boots all the time. And after he beat me and beat me and questioned and beat me, and I was saying, "I don't know, I don't know," then he sent me to the isolation cell with this guard of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he ask you while he was beating you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He asked us about the escape of that one, of Ekrem, who had fled, and that he'd slay all of us balijas, that we did not deserve even what we were getting there, this treatment which beggared imagination. I would say, "I don't know, man." "Of course, you know it all. You're organised well." "What organisation? Never crossed my mind. I barely live. I can't breathe." And the like. And then this one hits, that one hits, this blow, that blow, and there was just this one who did it. And I just happened to remember, Rasevic's deputy, he didn't get at me, perhaps because he knew me, but all the others beat me. And they said they'd kill us all, that all of us should be slain with no second thought, and things like that. And when he saw that I was all beaten up and battered, as soon as he'd beat one, he'd send him to the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you urinated blood afterwards. What kind of injuries did you actually sustain? What kind of injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I was beaten in the lower part of my back and he beat me for all he was worth. And to this day, I stopped bleeding in front but I still bleed from the back. And one can see it at all times. And when I go to defecate, one can see that. And I did rounds of physicians but there is no help.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many days did you need to recover from this beating so that you could move around?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I spent 12 days in the isolation cell. The first night they told us, "If we don't find him, you will be all killed tomorrow." But this Zeko was found, and I stayed 12 days in the isolation cell, lying down, suffering, and 12 days later a guard came and released me. But you can't do anything. We are trying to tell it to the Red Cross because it would happen in the beginning, when they -- there were interpreters, and I can prove it, and my head down to interpreters who were there in the late days of the camp. But the first interpreters who interpreted when we complained, they transmitted it to the staff. And the young men, those who complained, would disappear then. So I told myself, I mustn't complain, I mustn't anything. Because I had noticed it. We just noticed it. No sooner did someone complain than he'd be called out and then that young man would disappear. And they think while saying it, something will come out of it and something good will happen, but nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that anyone -- that others were as well beaten on this occasion. Did you actually see another detainee being beaten in that same spot?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I watched with my own eyes when Mandzo, whose nickname was Kelta, I don't know if that is his name, also beat him in front of my eyes but not for a long time, and said, "You go back to your room." I watched it with my own eyes. That is, I watched it with my own eyes because he was right in front of me. And at that moment, there were two of us. They began to beat this one, I watched it with my own eyes. What they said, "Did you have a part in this or not?" "No, no, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't." And he started sobbing and wailing and crying. And they let him go back into the room from which they had brought him. I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you were taken to the isolation cell. Did you see the other -- some other people being beaten in relation to this escape?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Every one of those men who were in the isolation cell was -- had been beaten, because, for instance, whenever they interrogate somebody, people scream and that is how they come. And the buildings are close to one, to each other, and they get to the isolation cell only within a matter of minutes so that we could hear the screams and yells and then they would come to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those -- how many detainees came to -- into your isolation cell on that day? How many were you altogether?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the exact number but 12 or 13. I would rather not give the exact number. I mean, I can't because I don't remember, but we were 12 or 13, and we were in the same room. And that night, we were ordered to stand, to stand up, after that beating. That is, we had to stand through the night and unless Zekovic was caught, that we would be shot the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these other 11 or 12 detainees who joined you in the isolation cell, were they roommates of Mr. Zekovic, or workmates?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They were -- in those rooms that were upstairs, they all had one key, that is one entrance, that is one next to the other. So from my room, from his room, and from the third, there were three or four rooms, two small and two large rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why were they locked together with you? What did these other 11 or 12 people have to do with Mr. Zekovic's escape, if at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Like this: They assumed that men who worked in the mechanical shop, that if they were beaten, then some of them would say that perhaps they knew, so they will beat them. If they say something, they will say something, or if not, nothing. And that's how it was. And I, because I was the shop steward of that room and some others, that they thought he had communicated with them, that he socialised with them, you know, in those rooms, that he talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you -- when they came to the isolation cell, did you see signs of beating on them, on these other people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Come, what do you mean, did not see? We all screamed and cried. Because they beat, as they beat me, they beat every one of them. Well, some more, some less, depends on how people succumbed, how people managed to shield themselves from blows. So some more, some less.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you were in the isolation cell for 12 days. Who released you from this isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: From the isolation cell, when you say, "Who released you," it is people from the administration who release you. And a guard took me out of the cell. But all the orders that come, they come from the administration, but there was a guard who was there, who took me out, the one who was on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when -- was Mr. Zekovic eventually captured?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Zekovic was eventually captured that morning, the next day, when they were to put us before the firing squad, and they brought him to the KP Dom, to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened when he was captured? What happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When Zekovic was captured, I stayed in the isolation cell - several of us were there - although he had been captured, so that I was in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the isolation cell even longer than Zekovic who had fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did -- when he was captured, did you have to go to the yard? Was there a kind of a gathering in the yard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When Zekovic was caught, the extremists -- I mean, I always call them extremists because after so many deaths, after so many horrible things that happened, I beg the pardon of the Court but these are extremists. They took him, they took Zekovic out into the yard, between these buildings, in this camp, and what would they say? This is what they said. The warden was there, Savo Todovic was there. I think Rasevic was too. And we were supposed to see an example as to how they treat us, how refined they were, and we all know what we had lived through and how many young people were killed until that moment. They thought that we were there in the camp, that we did not know anything. We were cattle for them. Nothing. And now they wanted to make themselves popular. They said, "Look, look at how we do not kill this Muslim people, how we do not mistreat the Muslim people, how we do not beat up these people, as people say." And we all passed by Zekovic, all of us, all of us who were in the rooms and also those who were in isolation cells, and of course we were all returned to the isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did this last? How long were you actually in front of Zekovic and the --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't long; short. Perhaps half an hour, an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that the warden was present. Who? Who was the warden at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: At that time, the warden was Milorad Krnojelac, and his deputy was Savo Todovic. So when Savo Todovic spoke, of course, the warden was there. They all looked so proud, as if they were ruling the world. As if they were people of goodwill, as if -- what was it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did Mr. Krnojelac say anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac just approved of the speech, because when Savo Todovic was delivering his speech, he addressed him too, and he was just voicing his approval, sort of saying, "Right. That's right. That's right," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean, "he addressed him too"? Who addressed whom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Savo Todovic was a bit -- I mean, he was speaking there, and then he was about half a metre away from Krnojelac, and then Savo Todovic, when he would speak, when he would say, "We are so good," et cetera, et cetera, then he would address Krnojelac. He would look at him, and Krnojelac would sort of go, "Right. Yes. Right."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krnojelac actually say something or did -- are you referring to body language when you say, "Right. Right"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He gave these signs, because all the preparations for the speeches and everything, all of that came from the administration. This man was speaking. He didn't have anything in writing. He wasn't reading. Then he was afraid that he might have missed something or whatever. So that's the way it was. Then he was just nodding away, sort of as if everything that he had been saying was just fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When we reached the prison, after awhile we were all taken to rooms where we were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I personally was interrogated by Slobodan Starovic. Actually, Vladicic was in that room. It is Vladicic's office. However, Starovic also came there out of curiosity, because he knew me. So both of them were there. Usually it was only one who was doing the interrogating - that's what others told me - but in this case, there were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Zoran Vladicic, who was he? What did he do before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Before the war, he was an investigator in the police, in the police, an investigator, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Starovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Starovic? He was a redundancy at the high school, so they gave him a job at the MUP. What he exactly did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were interrogated, were you accused of anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When they interrogated me, they said, "Are you a member of the SDA? Did you have any weapons? Did you have this? Did you have that?" I said, "I'm not a member of the SDA. I do not have any weapons. I haven't got a thing." And they wrote a record. I was so afraid that I signed this without having read a single letter of all of this, because I realised what I had fallen into, and I realised that they could do whatever they wanted to do, so I wasn't really interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you mistreated or threatened during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Neither one of them mistreated me, probably because they knew me well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you threatened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Starovic -- I don't know how I came there a second time. He said to me that they were taking everything from houses, from privately-owned houses, and Vladicic was saying, "No, no, no. Don't say things like that." So although at that time I did not really care about what they were doing to things, nevertheless, they were saying through all of that, "You're done."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were scared during the interrogation. Why were you so scared? What did you expect?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Every meeting with them meant either battery or death. That's what I was afraid of. Death from a firearm would have been fine, but in their case, death meant torture.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see other detainees return to your room being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did. Also at that very same interrogation, this and that and the other thing, we were forcing them to say things that were not true, because this battery and everything made people say whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's be precise. Whom did you see return from interrogation being beaten, in your room? Do you recall anyone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw -- I saw Professor Dzelilovic. Dzelilovic was his last name. He was beaten after that as well, and then he went missing. He was killed. I saw Vahida, the policeman. He was also -- later they were beaten too, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, wait. We have to talk about the persons one by one, and I have always some additional questions in relation to each person. So let's first handle one person and then go to the next. You said Dzelilovic -- Professor Dzelilovic you mentioned. Was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Professor Dzelilovic was not in my room. He used to come to the kitchen for meals. Then he would say to me -- I mean, I would say to him, "Can I do anything to help you?" He had come after I did. I said, "Can I do anything to help?" And he said, "I don't need a thing." Because they beat him there and also when he came to the camp. And his father came in, covered with blood. Then when they were being interrogated, then some of these extremist guards, as they were being brought in for an interrogation, those other guys pretended to be sort of moderate, but then these guards would come in and they would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest you answer my questions now very precisely, otherwise, we get lost. This Dzelilovic, did you see him with injuries? Did you see him being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did see them. I did see them. All of those who were beaten up had injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. When Professor Dzelilovic, when -- how often was he taken out of his room? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This is the way it was: When I saw Professor Dzelilovic in the kitchen, I saw him very briefly. He used to come to the kitchen, and then he disappeared; that is to say that everybody who was beaten up was killed after that, and they were nowhere to be seen after that. That is what we were told, and all of that proved to be true later on when we got out. His father was slaughtered in the KP Dom, his mother was slaughtered immediately, as soon as everything started, and his sister, let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Let's talk about -- please answer simply my question and not talk about other people, otherwise, we get confused. Did you see Mr. Dzelilovic with injuries or any signs of beating yourself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did. I did see him when he came to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And when you saw him in the kitchen, you saw injuries on him. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he got these injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He said -- I mean, I asked him, "How are you? How are you doing?" and he said to me, "Don't ask me a thing." He said to me that he couldn't even talk to me. Then I asked him -- I mean, since he had -- I asked him whether he had gone for an interrogation. He said, "Yes." So he told me that they had beaten him, and after that, he went missing. He was killed. After awhile, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was taken out from his room on another occasion and disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him -- did you see that he was called out on another occasion? Did you see him go somewhere or did you only hear about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me tell you. The group that came with him, they called out the names of that same group, and they were up there at the office, I mean, upstairs, and they beat them endlessly up there. We heard all of this. Both buildings could hear that because this is right across. Then after that, they disappeared. Now, how did we know that they disappeared? After that, those who had survived, they were taken to the bridge, the railway bridge that was nearby, and we heard shots. Then after the shots, we could hear - you can bring in any expert you want - you can hear something or somebody being thrown into the water, and that is what we assumed. One hundred per cent sure. That's what happened, and that's what the guards told us too, that that's exactly what had happened. So then we said that and they confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Look, stop. You really must answer the questions which were asked of you. You were asked a question three or four minutes ago. "Did you see that he was called out on another occasion? Did you see him go somewhere or did you only hear about it?" Now, that question can be answered yes or no. When you have answered that question, you will then be asked further questions -- please just wait a moment. You will be asked further questions to which you will be able to give this history. But unless you answer the questions and only the questions, the whole of these proceedings will be drawn out quite unnecessarily whilst counsel has to go back and start again. Now, please simply answer that question and wait for the next question before you tell us any more. Would you like to ask the question again, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Professor Dzelilovic being taken to somewhere within the compound on this day when he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was he taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see where he was going? Could you follow him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him going towards the gate where the offices are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you hear anything after he was taken into the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He was taken to the administration building, and then I heard moans and screams.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And could you locate -- could you hear, from the sounds, from which part of the administration building these moans and sounds were coming?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, from the second floor, the offices of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the plan 6/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you orient yourself on this plan?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. This down here is the lower part where you enter, and this up here are the rooms where we were locked up, and this left part was the torture cell for prisoners in those days. And then you take the hallway here, and then you would go to the staircase, and then you would go upstairs, and that's where the camp offices were. And then on -- here. Here. Sort of the middle of the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness -- witness, can you point with the pointer on the -- on the part of the administration building where you heard the sounds coming Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from, the sounds of screaming and moaning that you just described? Are you able to point that on this, in this section?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Here, in this part, on the second floor. This part here. You'd pass through here, here, through the door, and then there was this hall, and then through the hall, you would go to the staircase, and the upper part, there were these offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were moving around the pointer very much. Can you please put it on the spot and leave it there so that I can really identify it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Somewhere around here, here, sort of this area. I mean--

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you -- witness, you're pointing -- at the moment you're pointing -- witness, listen, please. At the moment, you were pointing at the canteen, at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection, Your Honour. He was not pointing at the canteen. He was pointing on the second floor above the canteen, because he said quite clearly, before this, that it was on the second floor of the administration building, and then he showed that it was above the canteen.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Above the canteen, there was nothing. There was just this theatre and cinema hall. I went through every one of the rooms as a prisoner because I was forced to do all this labour, all these different jobs. And now I cannot say, is this the canteen? This is the canteen. Now I see from here -- or rather I do not see. I mean I have to put on glasses in order to be able to see because if this is the canteen, then it is the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please put on your glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And just wait a moment, will you, so I can deal with the objection taken by Mr. Bakrac? Please, sir. Just wait a moment. Mr. Bakrac, you're quite right. He had said "on the second floor," and he was pointing at the word "canteen" in the map. That's very clear. Now, he's changed what he said before. It's a matter for you --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, sir. You can make what you can of that in cross-examination, but he has said two quite entirely different things. Your point was a good one. That's what he had said. But he was pointing at the word "canteen" and I think that's really all Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff meant. Now, can we just have one more question? And perhaps we will get the answer through by 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please put the pointer on the spot where you heard the sounds coming from, and leave it on that spot so that we can be clear.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the first room to the right-hand side of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said it's on the second floor. Do you count the first floor as -- the ground floor as the first floor, or what do you understand by "second floor"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On the second floor -- I mean, there is the ground floor and then this is one floor above the ground floor, because you have to walk up stairs. So it's the first floor above the ground floor. There are offices up there. It's before the canteen, before all of this, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So I think we have clarified this matter, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you proceed to the next question, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you had mentioned Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I would have to point out that Professor Dzelilovic, that's B-19 and C-7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned Vahida. Let me just -- what was the first name of Mr. Vahida?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't -- I knew but I forgot. I just know the last name. It sounded sort of strange to me: Vahida. That's how I remembered it. He was a town policeman before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vahida with injuries in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did. At that time, I did not work in the kitchen. At that time, I was in the rooms so I was in a room that directly faces the area where the detainees would pass in order to get to the kitchen to eat. So there would be one room, the other room, and all that. And I saw him, he was all beaten up, his face was swollen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see Mr. Vahida being taken later on, again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did see Vahida being taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where was he taken? Was it the same style as Mr. -- Professor Dzelilovic or was something different?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They took all of our inmates there to those offices up there. I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty now whether it's this office or that office, but at any rate, it was upstairs. It was upstairs. That's where there was battery, if that's the way I should put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When Mr. Vahida was taken, did you hear the same sounds that you had just described in relation to Mr. Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Whenever they would call out someone's name, three or four minutes after that, we would hear moans. Sometimes it would be in the morning, sometimes in the afternoon, sometimes in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you hear such moans when Mr. Vahida was taken to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The same, the same moans. Somebody was louder, others would lose their voice, and others would be even louder. So that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him return?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There was no return from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Just a minute. Once I saw him. I saw him return. He was all beaten up as he was passing there to go to eat. And after that, he was taken away. I don't know when that happened, but he went missing and there has been no trace of him since.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Schedule C-27 and also the incident 5.29 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a nurse Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mandzo, I know his last name. He's the son of a house painter whom I knew personally. And I know Mandzo, too; I mean the son.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being beaten in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him. At that time I was in that room. One room next to the other. When the guards took him and another man, Dzanko -- Cankusic, I saw them being taken away and we heard them being beaten then. And then after this beating, they came to the rooms. One came. I think he was Mandzo. His face was totally disfigured, all cut up. And the doctor who was in the room then, his name is Berberkic, he used a thread and needle to sew up his face. I also saw his feet, all swollen. Once they would be taken out for beatings, they would come back unrecognisable. It is unbelievable, unbelievable. So I saw the way they returned because I was there in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It is 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we resume, I remind the parties that we're not sitting tomorrow afternoon because of the Celebici judgement being given in this courtroom. There's been a further incursion upon our sitting times. Judge Mumba and I have to attend a special meeting of the Bureau at 9.00. However, with the cooperation of everybody who looks after us here, we've been able to change the sitting time to start at 10.00 in the morning. We'll sit from 10.00 until 11.30 and then from 12.00 until 1.30, and that will be the same three hours for a morning hearing, so we only lose the afternoon time. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you do not know the first name of this person Mandzo. During your testimony you mentioned a Kelta Mandzo. That's not the same person, or is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that this incident relates to an Emir Mandzo, B-37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that there is also another person, there was another victim involved in this, and you said that it was a Dzanko. Do you know the first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Dzanko was a salesman near Foca, and I met him only after he arrived in the camp, because we were in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when he returned, what did you see? Did you see any injuries on this person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Both came into the room one after the other, right one after the other, perhaps a minute between them, and one could see on their heads and on their legs how they had been beaten, both of them. This one had a face cut, as I told you already. The doctor, Berberkic, sewed it with a thread. Mandzo was worse beaten. And I know he was a medical technician, and I know he was at the medical centre in Foca. He was beaten worse. The other one was slightly older, and perhaps those swellings wouldn't have -- were to appear because everything would have burst, his legs and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes this to be the victim B-18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a -- in the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned a lawyer, Cedic, that you also met in the KP Dom. Was this person beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Cedic, when I first met him in the camp, told us that even before he'd arrived in the camp, he had had to eat I don't know how many kilograms of salt and been beaten, and in the camp, he was called out and all trace of him is lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When this person Cedic was -- this lawyer Cedic was called out in the camp, did you hear afterwards the sound of beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: About this Cedic, I'm not sure and I cannot testify about him, but he told the whole room that even before he had arrived in the camp he had been beaten and ill-treated, and after he left, all trace of him was and is lost, when he was called out to come out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that this is the person B-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you are -- did you know a Nurko Nisic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I knew Nurko Nisic well. A relative of mine was married to him, even. He worked for the SUP, the police as it was called. He used to be an investigator before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see this person with injuries in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him personally with injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you see him with injuries? Was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, not in my room, but whenever those beatings happened, we were always at the window, that is, some distance from the windows, because we dared not approach them close, to see what would happen to them. And he was all swollen, he was all bruised. And he was also killed later on, that is, is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken on several occasions for beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. He went for beatings repeatedly and the last time, I don't know the date because I don't remember dates and I cannot really say that, he screamed so much when they beat him, and after that, in the evening, they took them away and threw them off the Drina bridge which is very close, that is right behind our dormitories. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said he screamed so much. Does that mean you recognised his voice when he was screaming?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: We recognised all -- I recognised all people I know, I met, that I knew. I recognised the voices of all those people whom I know well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's C-19 and incident 5.27 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: And this selfsame Halim, I saw him being taken out, and I recognised his voice too. And he was killed also. And after he was killed, that is ill-treated and beaten in those offices, he was killed and found. I learnt afterwards, and I also attended the funeral, if I may call it that, in Sarajevo, when Amer Masovic [phoen] and others found his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see Halim Konjo being taken on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: On several occasions, oh, yes, on several.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Invariably, whenever one of them, whoever it was, whoever went there, he'd come back with injuries, and that includes him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour it's C-13 and B-33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the Rikalo brothers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I met brothers Rikalo in the camp. And another relative of theirs, that relative I knew better because he was a waiter in the town. And brothers Rikalo, I only met in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this waiter, what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I only know the last names. I don't know their name. I know he was -- I know his last name was Rikalo and I know he lived in Cohodor Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any of those three, the brothers or the waiter -- did you see any of them with injuries in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw those two brothers Rikalo. Allegedly they worked at the Tjentiste 27 kilometres away. I saw them with injuries several times. And they also then disappeared and were killed, and this relative too, but not as much as those two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness referred to Schedule C, 21 to 23 and Schedule B, 45 to 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a Nail Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I knew Nail Hodzic too. He was a taxi driver for a while, and then worked for Focatrans company.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see or hear anything in relation to him concerning beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He was taken out likewise, in the beginning, several times, and all trace of him is lost, which means that he was killed too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Mustafa Kuloglija?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, Mustafa Kuloglija, yes, I know him too. He lived in the locality of Aladza, and he was also taken out several times and he disappeared, was killed. He was taken out to be beaten. That's how we put it over there. And after that, he disappeared and was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever have a discussion with one of the prison staff about this person, Mustafa Kuloglija?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did talk to the head of the -- to the head cook. His name was Krnojelac. He lived in the same building in Aladza. Kuloglija found this on him or found this at his place, so that I saw and realised what was in store for him, because they invented, they made up things as it suited them for individual people, and they sort of explained it to themselves that these people had to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person, the victim is C-15.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Krunoslav Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Krunoslav Marinovic. Yes, I know him as well. He is a man of Croat ethnicity who came to the camp all beaten up. And Krunoslav Slabinac, beaten as he was, he was ill-treated everywhere, and after that, they killed him and he is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the last name of this Croat Krunoslav?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know he was married to a countrywoman of ours nee Gagovic. I think his last name was Marinovic. Marinovic, I believe it is. He was married to our woman. He was a TV repairman in the town, and he was married to our countryman [as interpreted] whose last name was Gagovic, but he's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's C-17.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Hamid Bico?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Hamid Bico. Yes, I know him well too. He had a restaurant in Donje Polje, and he was a policeman after that, before the war. He was also beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: And after that, all trace of him is lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he taken only once for beating or several times?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Several times. He also watched it with us and also talked with our man, but he -- I don't know what. Anyone who had something in the town, they beat them and battered them and killed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was: You said that he was beaten several times. Did you see him with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of injuries do you remember, if any?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Injuries. They had injuries, but they were protected down there, but on the head there were -- once saw injuries. And whoever they took, they came back with injuries on their head. The only one who did not have injuries on his head was Ekrem Zekovic. All the others had injuries in addition to all the other injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you see Hamid Bico when he had injuries on his head?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: All in the passage. Even at the time when I was in the kitchen, I saw that he was injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-2 and B-5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz. I know that you mentioned name, but all of a sudden I know well -- I know him well. He was the shop steward in the Visoko shop in Foca. He arrived with Marinovic, and he was all black. And when they undressed, both of them -- and I managed to steal some onions from the kitchen in order to apply them to their wounds. They were barely alive when they arrived. They could not move. They could do nothing. And that's the one, Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he taken -- within the KP Dom, while detained there, was he taken away for beatings on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: They were taken out, two of them. I don't know myself when they were taken out and killed. Pressure was brought against them immediately, so that they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You're referring to Hamid Bico and Zulfo Veiz when you say, "The two of them"? Do you mean these two or which two?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. Zulfo Veiz and Marinovic, and Bico is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And Mate Ivancic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honours, I just forgot to mention. Zulfo Veiz, that's C-29 and 5.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mate Ivancic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mate Ivancic from civilian days. When I saw him in the camp I said, "What are you doing here?" "Right. I understand that they are killing us, the Muslims, as they are killing Croats, because that is the objective of the extremists." And I thought that he was a Serb, and so I asked him. And he said, "I am a Croat too." And he was taken out several times and beaten and finally killed and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the Cankusic brothers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know brothers Cankusic. Well, I know them so-so, but I knew their father well. They were also, right at the beginning, taken out, beaten and killed, and to this day, their father and family mourn them in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see them being taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw all of that. They did nothing. They said they were taking them out, just like that, to ask them a few questions. But we knew why they were taking them away, and when they came back, it was all clear as daylight to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These two brothers are C-3 and C-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Seval Soro?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Soro were -- just a moment. I can't really remember the names, but they were Soros 1, 2, 3, 4. Four Soro families. One was a driver, another Soro was an electrician, a third Soro was perhaps the elementary school, and one was a technician at Brod, three kilometres from Foca, so that I know the last name, but their first names I can't, and all four of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any of the four Soros being taken for beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw the Soro who was a driver, and I saw Soro the electrician being taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a Fuad Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, I know Fuad Mandzo too. He comes from Donje Polje. He's quite a young man, and I used to know him before. Let me just tell you about an event, about an incident. There were several people called Mandzo and when they wanted to beat this one, Fuad Mandzo, several times got Kelta Mandzo, and Kelta kept saying, "I'm not the one, I'm not the one," because they thought it was Fuad Mandzo. And that is how it happened. But besides, they also beat him badly and killed him, and then he disappeared, several times and it was right in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Fuad Mandzo is C-16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Enes Uzunovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know Enes Uzunovic because he was a married to Halim Konjo's sister. And I knew Halim Konjo well and he told me that he was his brother-in-law. He was a medical technician, and he was also in the early days taken out, beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person Alija Altoka?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Alija Altoka, I know that last name, yes. I know him. He comes from the locality of Aladza, and he was also taken out, killed and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me; beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's C-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Granov Adil?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Adil Granov is a young man. That is, I could be -- he could be my son. I knew him personally and I also knew his family. And he was taken out, beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was his profession, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He worked in the wire factory, an engineer. Whether a mechanical engineer or an electrical engineer, I don't really know, but he was an engineer. I think he was an electrical engineer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the person C-9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Munib Veiz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes. I know Munib Veiz too. Well, Munib Veiz, Munib Veiz -- just a moment. Munib Veiz. I know him but I just can't recall his face. Yes, I know the name. All those others, I seem to be seeing them right now. All those others, I seem to be seeing their faces right now. Now, it comes to me. Couldn't it be that Munib Veiz was beaten at the same time with Kruno Marinovic? Now, I'm not quite -- Munib Veiz? I think he was a policeman. If it's not the other one, then Munib Veiz was a policeman. Chestnut hair. Munib Veiz. Munib Veiz. I apologise to the court if I -- if this is not 100 per cent correct but I think that this Munib Veiz was a policeman, and every policeman who worked for the police before the war was taken out, was beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you also mentioned Zulfo Veiz. Who of the two is the policeman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, Zulfo. Munib Veiz, Munib Veiz. Zulfo Veiz I think worked in a shop. Those are the two where I got a little bit -- Zulfo, Zulfo Veiz. Zulfo Veiz, I think it was, because both had the same last name and I -- all I know is surnames. And one was a policeman and the other one was a foreman in a shop, and I know their last names. I think Zulfo Veiz was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see -- you have already described that this policeman Veiz was beaten on several occasions and you remember that he came --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He would come back and, after he came back, he was called out and disappeared and was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the shop owner Veiz, what did you see happen to the shop owner?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He came all black from blows, and after a short period of time, he disappeared, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he in your room when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He was in our room when he was beaten, and after that, I went to another room, and I was told -- I asked, "Well, what about Marinovic? How about this one? How are they?" Gone. Missing. Killed. And I was in another room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Munib Veiz is C-28 and B-59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Kemal Tulek?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Kemal Tulek, I know him. His brother was a pilot in the Yugoslav People's Army. When he was brought from this place which is near Foca, he spent all the time in a dungeon where they beat him, and I asked to take food there sometimes so I could see who was there. So I saw him in this isolation cell. I personally saw him. After that, I think he was killed and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This isolation cell that you mentioned, in which building was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The isolation cell was in building 2, not the first one but the second one, and the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see -- when you went there, did you see injuries on Mr. Tulek?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not only on Tulek. Every one of them. They could not have come to an isolation cell without having been beaten up, so, yes, I did see injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see when Mr. Tulek was taken for the last time -- away for the last time and did not return?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Tulek also disappeared. I can't say for sure how long his suffering went on, for several months perhaps, I didn't know when he was taken out because they would take people out during the night, but all of a sudden he was no longer there. He was killed, and disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's C-25.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a Ramo Dzendusic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Ramo Dzendusic? Ramo Dzendusic was a salesperson, Dzendusic. Again, when I say Ramo, I'm not very good at names. I don't know people very well by their first names but Dzendusic was in the first room where Mandzo was and where all of us were at first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see him being beaten? Did you ever see him with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me say straight away that Dzendusic -- if you mean the one that I mean, I saw injuries, but if this is a person who was nearby, who was manager of the shop in Josanica -- let me say one more thing. There is this neighbourhood called Tabaci which is a bit further away and that person from there was also a salesperson, and this man was beaten so badly that he hanged himself in this isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But let's stick with the person Dzendusic. You said you saw him being beaten. Was he in your room where you were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: If it is this salesperson from Josanica, he was in my room. However if it's this salesperson who was from Tabaci near Foca, I was not with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are talking about the salesperson Dzendusic that you mentioned. Was he beaten in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness said that both of the Dzendusics he knew were salespersons.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the last names, the last names are very similar. One was Dzankusic or something like that. These last names are very similar so I can't really tell. I actually saw both of them. This salesperson from Josanica and this salesperson from Tabaci. Now, I cannot know the name for sure. If you were to tell me where this salesperson was from, then I would be able to tell you. However, I saw both of them being tortured and killed and they were taken in an unknown direction and killed, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, if I may deal with your objection, he did say earlier on that he wasn't very clear about the names, the surnames. He said, "I don't know people very well by their first names but," and then he gave the name, "was in the first room where Mandzo was." And then later on, he says, "However, if it's the salesperson who was from" somewhere near Foca, "I was not with him." And then the question was, "We are talking about the salesperson that you mentioned." Now I'm not sure what the basis of your objection was. It was the salesperson that the Prosecution was following up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said that both of the Dzendusics he knew were salespersons from Tabaci and from this other place, Josanica, and then the question that followed said, "And now this salesperson that you mentioned," but both are salesmen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You only want identified from which one, from which area?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which salesperson the Prosecutor has in mind. I mean, which is the salesperson that the Prosecutor refers to as "that salesperson," this one or that one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you might have already had it cleared up for you by what the witness said while I was trying to listen to what Mr. Bakrac was saying. I wish he would not interfere with the processes of the Court. But I think you'd better sort out, make it very clear with the witness which one you intend him to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, the salesperson from Josanica, is that the person who was in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see him being beaten in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did you see on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He had swellings on his face, and we asked him, "What happened? Did they beat you in the lower part too?" Then he said, "Yes," and that his legs and feet were swollen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this person, this salesperson from Josanica, was he taken on another occasion as well and beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Soon afterwards, both were taken out and they were beaten, of course, and then they disappeared and were killed, because everybody who was taken out was beaten up and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You said this other salesperson from Tabaci. How was he killed? You mentioned -- maybe I misunderstood you, but you mentioned that someone hanged himself.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The other salesperson from Tabaci. He could not take all of this, all these beatings and everything, and he hanged himself. That salesperson from Tabaci, from up there, he hanged himself in an isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Oh, straight away. I told you, whatever happened, even outside, we knew. We knew all these cases immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first -- the Prosecution believes that the first person -- the first salesman from Josanica has the name Dzendusic and is mentioned in B-20 and C-8. The other salesperson, the Prosecution believes that it is -- it's actually the person number 6 on Schedule C with the name Juso Dzamalija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sure that the transcript writers will be very pleased to get the document -- please, sir, will you be quiet while we're speaking. Please. It's very difficult for us to speak if we continually hear you speaking over us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's been a lot of trouble with the transcript in relation to that name, so now that you give them the reference, that will help. Yes. Now, Mr. Bakrac, did you want to object to something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I don't know how the Prosecutor can say C-6 when that person is Juso Dzamalija, not Dzendusic as this man said, and is not a salesperson at all, but he is an employee of the military department. So the witness did not mention that person at all. What is the Prosecutor thinking of? Why does the Prosecutor even think of C-6 in this context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you will have every opportunity of pointing that out to us in the course of your submissions at the end of the trial, that the facts upon which the Prosecution relies has no relationship at all to the passage in the indictment which they referred to us. It's not really an objection. All we're being told by the Prosecution is that that's what they say establishes that allegation in the indictment. You may very well be right it has nothing to do with it, but we can't decide that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise to you. However, in the system that I come from, this is not allowed. So that's why I thought that perhaps I was acting out of an abundance of caution, as you have pointed out several times. So I sort of signalled now. I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I am not criticising you. I am just pointing out that that is a matter we can't resolve on an objection to a statement made by the Prosecution in court. Will you proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a Mehmed Sofradzija or Mesa Sofradzija?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I do. I do personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Was he in the camp, and did you see him with injuries or being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Mesa Sofradzija, he was staying with his brother who was a military man in Novi Sad. A warrant was issued by these extremists that he be taken prisoner and brought to the Foca camp. He was brought in from Novi Sad to the Foca camp where he was beaten up. He spent more time in an isolation cell than he did in any other room. They did all sorts of things to him. He was not in my room, but I saw him. I saw him before he was taken to the isolation cell. I did not see him in the isolation cell, but I saw him beaten up while he was still in the room. Actually, when they had just brought him from the offices, when they brought him to the room. Then he was taken to the isolation cell where he was beaten up. Because when people were beaten up in isolation cells, you could hear everything. You could hear a fly. He was also killed, and no one's heard of him since. I knew him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. personally. That's why I know his nickname Mesa. I know that he worked in the municipality. I know everything about him, where he's from; everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is referred to in B-52.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Rasim Kajgana?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Rasim Kajgana? I knew him personally as well. He had shops of his own. They brought him from Montenegro, from Pljevlje. He was in my room for a short while. Then they took him away and killed him.
