Since he knew Mojovic who had been killed, he knew him personally, and he begged him to let him go, to ask the people from the administration to let him go, but nothing came out of that. So they took him away and killed him. And everybody who had anything in Foca was killed except for me. (redacted). but perhaps it is God who saved me. Maybe I won't last for a very long time after this, but I have been spared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you see Mr. Kajgana with injuries in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I did not see him with injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken and did you hear anything afterwards, I mean, screams or the sound of beatings in relation to this particular victim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He disappeared. He disappeared. He went from the room; he disappeared. He was killed. There's been no trace of him since.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But did you hear the sound of beatings when he was taken? This was my question.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No. No, I don't seem to remember that, because when they took people out, sometimes I was in the room and sometimes I wasn't, because sometimes we would be out somewhere in the field, working, whatever. So I don't seem to remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's B-32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know Avdo Mehmedspahic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I knew Avdo Mehmedspahic personally. (redacted). He was also beaten up, and he spent all his time there in the isolation cell. And I saw what he looked like. They also brought him later, after I had come, and I saw what he looked like. He looked bad. After that, he was also killed, and he disappeared. He was at the KP Dom, in the camp, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you saw what he looked like. What did he look like? What did you see on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, how should I put this to you, what his face looked like, when one of his lips was cut and the other was swollen? I have no words to express myself. I have no words to express that. He looked bad, really bad. When a man is beaten up -- well, I have no words for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see him in the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I personally saw him in the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the person B-40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a family or detainees with the last name Hadzimesic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I do. These are two brothers from the Aladza neighbourhood. One was a driver, and the other one worked in the accounting department of Focatrans.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know their first names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Only Hadzimesic. Although they were from Foca, they were youngish men, so I only knew their last name. They are younger. They were younger than I was, and until the present day, I do not know the names of people who are younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any of those two being beaten or with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The one who worked in Focatrans. He was mistreated more than the other one who was a driver at the medical centre. They were really mad at this enterprise of Focatrans, so they took him and the others out several times. They questioned them and beat them up, and finally he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that it's the person under B-24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you see detainees being beaten in the kitchen or in front of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: At that moment, I was not working in the kitchen. I was working outside, cutting firewood that came in from the outside. Then our people were lined up for lunch. A few persons came in wearing something like military uniforms, and they started mistreating our people. I was a bit further away, perhaps about 50 metres away. I did not hear what they were saying to them, but I saw them being beaten, one by one, on the legs and on the head. So we who were a bit further off were in a mousehole, as our people tend to say, because we were afraid that everybody would get killed, us included.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall who was among the victims of this incident? Do you recall any?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: At that moment I knew, but there were several of them. There were several of them, actually. This was this group, and then they'd slap one in the face, they'd hit another one on the legs, and then we fled. We tried to hide behind the trees because we thought that this was the end of us. I can just tell you one thing: We thought every minute that that would be the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were guards present when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The guards. When the extremists would come in, those guards would become tiny or, rather, they would not. They would figure prominently as well. They would start doing the same thing. Perhaps three or four of them -- no, perhaps up to three of them, the same ones all the time. So they really welcomed this. They were really pleased when they saw these other ones beating people up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We have to be very specific when we speak about specific incidents. I want to know if on this occasion when you saw the detainees being beaten by soldiers, on this occasion, did you see any guards present?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The guards -- whenever anybody would go out into the yard, the guards who were on duty would be there at every moment, whoever would go out into the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall when -- on this specific occasion here, what the guards did?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not then. We're talking about this specific occasion. They would just sort of stand aside and pretend that nothing was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was that the only incident of such kind where soldiers from outside beat detainees at lunchtime or did you see such occurrences on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way: From the town of Foca, out of the extremists who were in Foca, at any time of day and night, they would come and take people out and kill them, whoever they wanted to. Thirdly, at Brioni, that is three kilometres away, where we worked, the Vojvoda from Medjurecje, I cannot remember his name right now, with two other Vojvodas, came to the bridge where we were working. We were cleaning Brioni. And house painters were using oil to clean the bridge. When they came up, then this man said, "Atif" -- Atif is a lawyer from Foca -- Zelenovic, Zelenovic is the Vojvoda's name. And then he said to this man, "Come here." Then he said, "I have to report to the guard," and he cursed him sort of like, "What guard are you talking about?" They didn't care. So he took this oil, greased him all over with it, kicked him up, and then this river where they were working, that was the river of Cehotina, and had he thrown him into the Cehotina, he could have drowned. So that was that particular case. Then also let me tell about other cases where there was this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We cannot talk about each incident. We have to focus on the incident in the indictment. And I just want to know from you, this incident you describe where soldiers from outside came and beat up, lining -- or prisoners in the yard in relation to meals, did that occur several times or did you see it only once?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Several times. Once I saw when a Vojvoda came - he called himself a Vojvoda - and then there was this man there called Rasim, he wanted to beat him up. He started slapping him in the face. And he said to me, "Do you know him?" And I said, "Yes, I know him." I said, "Please, please don't do that." So he slapped him in the face a few times, kicked him up a bit. So that was another one of these cases of persons coming in from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see a handicapped person being beaten at lunchtime, in the canteen or in front of the canteen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I personally saw when there was this deaf-mute man on the staircase. I think that the policeman's name is Pljevaljcic. He was really beating him badly, kicking him. And in addition to all of that, the policeman called Burilo said, "I am going to beat this man so badly that I'm going to make him speak." And that's the way it was. And that's the kind of thing that was done to people. Let everybody know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this person, this handicapped person, this deaf-mute person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I don't, I don't. The first time I saw the man in my life, and I didn't ask later on what his name was because he didn't really mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he the only deaf-mute person, detainee, in the camp or did you meet others?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: There was another deaf-mute from Donje Polje. There was a mental patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm talking about the deaf-mute person.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I don't think -- yes, I think he was the only one deaf and mute. From what I know, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know his profession?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: His profession was -- I decipher it through the guards because they said in the yard, "He pretends to be a shepherd and yet informs Bosnian government" or something, and that was in front of us, and he was brought in from some mountains. What he was, I don't know, but he said, "Oh, he pretends to be a shepherd. He is trying to pull the wool over his eyes." But he was quite aged. I really don't know what he could --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him later on, this --

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: He is missing too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution believes it's the person B-35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let's -- you said that you were detained quite some time. Do you recall when you were released from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: May I describe my release in a few words? In October, we were told that we would be taken to be exchanged. And they brought us to Kula. It is a few kilometres from Sarajevo. And a Vojvoda with his Chetniks from Miljevina came, and the guards, the sentries, those who were with us, they simply stepped aside. And he said, "You all back, you will all be killed." And they took us back to Miljevina. It's a locality near Foca. Well, after that, from the administration of the camp, people came and they talked to him and this and that, and if they didn't set us free, then their combatants, as they called it, would not be released, and so they took us back to Kula. We spent waiting at Kula that night, and then early in the morning, everybody was exchanged, and some 12 or 13, I don't know the exact number, stayed behind, in Kula, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when were you exchanged? How many days later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: A few days. Again, ill-treated there but they didn't tread on us at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I you said that someone from the administration of the KP Dom came to Miljevina to sort the matter out. Who was that who came?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I think -- no, like this. The warden at that time was Sekulovic. He was the warden then. No, it wasn't Rasevic. What was his name? Arsenic came with him, and yet another one who worked there before. Can't remember his last name but he also worked formerly in what was called the KP Dom and then he also worked in the camp later. They came. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me briefly address some other persons who, from the KP Dom. You -- who was the warden before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Before the war, the warden was -- I'm not really sure, I'll tell you, but his last name was Arsenic Radojica. Radojica was his first name. I think his last name was Arsenic. He was the warden before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this person, this pre-war warden, did you see him in the prison while you were confined there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I used to see him in the prison, like this. He was up in the office of the prison for a short while. His wife worked there too, and his wife worked there before the war also. Then he stepped on a mine. Mojovic; that was his name. He was in charge of the farm which is some three kilometres away. That was the farm of the KP Dom, that is the camp. Now, when Mojovic was killed by a mine, Radojica was transferred up there and he became the head of that farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you -- where did you see Mr. Radojica, this pre-warden. How long did you see him in the prison compound as such and when in Brioni?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: You mean before the war or during the war? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the war. Did you see Mr. Radojica, did you see him during the war in the prison compound where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw him in the compound too but I knew that he was not the warden. Everybody knew that, because those men who were so emaciated, and I was one of them, but, well, I was -- I had my pride and never wanted to beg anyone for anything. Besides, I saw what they were doing, killing, torturing and so forth, so he asked who can he talk about something --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We have to be very focused. Where else did you see Mr. Radojica?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Radojica as follows. I saw him in the compound's yard. Then I saw him up where I worked at the farm, Brioni, and he was the chief there, and his deputy was a veterinarian and deputy's deputy was Slobodan Kunarac, whom I also knew well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are not talking about these other people now, we are talking about Mr. Radojica. How do you know he was the chief in Brioni? Did you talk to him about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Oh, come. He is not a person who ever sought popularity but that one, Kunarac, and the veterinarian, whenever he turned up, if they had forgotten to do something, then they would say, "Oh, here comes the boss. Here comes the warden" -- no, not the warden, the warden was in the KP Dom. And this was the farm and it was a kind of a department of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also mentioned a person Mojovic who actually was the -- who was there before Radojica. What was he doing? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Head of the farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long was he the head of the farm?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: When I speak, I cannot say. He was -- for several months, I think. I cannot really tell you from two but he was there for several months, and after several months, he left with drivers who were Serb convicts, and near Ustikolina they drove over a mine and he was killed and the driver survived. And after that, Radojica took his place as the head there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already described that you saw a Mr. Krnojelac on the first day on your arrival and he was wearing civilian clothes. When you saw him later on, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Later on, he had a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of military uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No rank insignia or anything. Well, like those that the reservists wore before, no rank markings, anything, just plain reservists, those who had no ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall when Mr. Krnojelac was replaced?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Again, to give you the date, I can't say. He was there in the beginning for a long time and a few months before the end, before we were exchanged, Zoran Sekulovic replaced him and I knew him well too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with Mr. Sekulovic after he was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Knowing Sekulovic well -- and there is faculty of theology in Foca where there was the women's prison before the war, and wherever something had to be done, to be cleaned or whatever, we had to do it, so we were doing it up there, and Sekulovic came. And I said -- no, he said, Hello. Had he not said Hello, I wouldn't have said anything to him, but he did say Hello, so I told him, "Sekulovic, come, is there any possibility? Will you check there if I am being charged with anything or something?" And Sekulovic tells me, "First I have to get my neighbour, my next-door neighbour out." Sekulovic is from a village 12 kilometres away, Atif Jasarevic. So he says, "First I have to get him out and then your turn will be." And that's how it was. First he let Jasarevic go and then there was exchange for all of -- there was the exchange for all of us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Savo Todovic already. What was his exact function in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not getting the interpretation. Savo Todovic's position, he was deputy warden in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In a prior statement that you gave to the Prosecutor's office, you said that Savo Todovic had as much authority or even more than Mr. Krnojelac. What did you mean? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: By this I meant that Savo Todovic behaved -- well, our people say he behaved inappropriately even for crazy man. Savo Todovic was given a stick and he used it to vent whatever he felt like venting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw him in the prison, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Savo Todovic. Savo Todovic, well, those others called him "Bunda fur coat" because he always had a sheepskin on him, always. Never stopped. Be it summer, be it winter, he always had a sheepskin and boots.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides the coat, did he wear civilian clothes or did he wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Later on. Later on, yes, he wore a military uniform, but that sheepskin, that was olive-green/grey, and one could see them worn by civilians and everybody else. The place was full of those sheepskins, but it was the olive-green/grey colour. They called it driver's sheepskin. Must have got it -- must have pinched it from some former driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he gave tasks to you when you were working, and he was actually in charge of this. Did he also give tasks to the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: And Serb prisoners. And Serb prisoners, yes. He assigned tasks to Serb prisoners too, because we could see them go to their rooms, and they all gather around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned in the beginning you wrote down two names of staff members that talked about Mr. Krnojelac being the warden and Mr. Todovic being the deputy. Did they say anything else about Mr. Todovic's role or was it that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: This is how they put it: If we -- "If one of them sees us with you, he can only see how we ill-treat you, how we beat you. But if they see us talking to you" -- the war had already begun, Gorazde was already defending itself, and it is 33 kilometres away from Foca. It was defending itself, when they saw how much was burnt and killed over here. So that whichever of them behaved like that, they would send him to the front line straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During your time of detention at the KP Dom, this detention, how did this affect your physical health, except for the beating and the physical injuries that you already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: All that I went through there, when I left and was free again, I suffered a stroke and I spent a whole month in coma, because not only the starvation, I also had a wound, and I could not control -- I could not contain myself, and I also bled. I've already told you about this. Then the sugar content rose in my blood. So that I really have nothing of my life any more, nothing. I can't do anything physically. And my wife often says, "Why don't you do something? Why don't you find some job?" But when she saw it all, then she closes her mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about your psychological state of health? Was it also affected and did you suffer later on as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me tell you, when I entered this courtroom, changed, it changed a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean, Witness? You mean your physical health changed or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I suffered major consequences. The Court can appoint a commission to examine me, to see that I am telling the truth, full truth about it. I've become very short-tempered. I've come to dislike myself even.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I am Mihajlo Bakrac, and I'm one of the counsel for the defendant Milorad Krnojelac. Are you up to being asked more questions or ...

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: No, no. I'm quite up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you said in the KP Dom they called you balija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Not only me, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you say it's a pejorative term?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: If I tell you "Bor" and you come from Serbia, from Belgrade, would you feel offended? Well, perhaps not, but to me, yes, because everybody knows what I am by ethnicity, and words which are derogatory, which are expletives, that is how I understand them. Because they said, "Balijas, we shall loot your property. We shall burn your property. We shall kill you," everywhere. In canteens and working sites, everywhere. They simply did not tread on us, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. But can you tell me what the word "balija" means?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, now you can turn this word this way and that way. Perhaps you've read something and perhaps you picked out the best way that suits you, but why didn't they call us balijas before, regardless of what you think of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not here to argue with you. I'm here to ask you some questions. So will you please wait for me to ask the question, to have it interpreted, and answer me. My question, my specific question was: Will you tell me what the word "balija" means.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: And I'm telling you, you've studied the word. I've never studied it, not in the least to ask myself what the word "balija" was. But what I do know is, and they play non-stopped music in that camp, "Alija, I don't like you because you're balija." Now, if that means something to you. I supposed it does. And I guess I've told you all I have to tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look, sir, Mr. Bakrac said to you a few moments ago that you should pause at the end of his question before you commence the answer. Let me explain to you what the situation is. What you are both saying is being translated into both English and French. The interpreters have to listen to the question and then interpret it, so that they are still interpreting the question at the time you hear it finish. When you both speak the language, you, obviously, are not hearing the interpretation. But if you answer the question straight away, then the interpreters can't catch up. So please will you pause for a substantial period after the question before you answer it. Now, that's the first warning I want to give you. The second one is: Please do not try to argue with counsel. Mr. Bakrac is here appearing for the accused. He has a job to do. He is not personally involved in the case in any way. So don't argue with him. Just try to answer his questions. If you don't understand them, don't hesitate to say so, but please remember we are here to work out what happened. We are not hear to listen to arguments. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Always when you answered questions in the -- they were during the examination-in-chief, you always said "Chetniks," everybody "Chetniks, thieves, murderers." Is that the -- are these the words that you commonly use for Serbs, and it is also pejorative to use such words to describe Serbs or is it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: I shall say it like this: I spoke about Serbs who left, who did not want the war in Foca and who went to Novi Sad. I also spoke about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. honest Serbs, about Serbs of integrity who stayed behind but who refused to take up knives or rifles or any other weapons. So I'm not referring to all Serbs. But when I say "Chetniks, butchers," they're not all Serbs. And I never said all Serbs were that. But in Foca and everywhere else, everybody knows who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you now bitter about those Serbs in Foca who never took up arms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Of course I am bitter. I have a bitter -- I'm bitter about all the butchers. You can't even imagine how bitter I feel about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I can understand how bitter you feel about them. And Muslims in Foca, did they have any arms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Let me tell you, when the gunfire began by the extremists who started it all, a group in Donje Polje began to defend themselves. To me, personally, people who participated in that fighting on the Serb side, they thought that some passages had been made there or something, but nothing of the kind, nothing of the sort happened, which means that a group tried to save their own lives, and that locality is called Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Muslims began to arm themselves as early as 1991 and that they also formed their detachments or, rather, their military formations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: When the extremists said, "We shall slay you all, we shall kill all of you if you vote for the sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were as -- we are armed so well and we've got the whole Yugoslav army to back us," to instil fear in those who said that, our men said, and they spoke about this publicly around coffee shops and other places, "Oh, we've got arms this. Oh, we've also got this. We've also got that," to put some fear into those extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which means that Muslims never had anything of this and they only talked big to intimidate the other side, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: That was the beginning of the war, because I was there personally, and that's how it was, and that was the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What does it mean, "the beginning of war"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-73
utterances.text: The beginning of extremists, the beginning of torching, who started it all. I won't now talk who started it all, because everybody knows who started it all, who butchered, who torched not only businesses but also houses of the Muslim people. And did any church in Foca perish? No. Did any Serb perish when those extremists started the war? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I know that that is a provocative answer, but may I remind you that we are not here to determine who was responsible for starting the war. That is simply irrelevant to anything this Tribunal has to decide. We have to determine whether there was an attack upon the civilian population and in the course of it did these things happen, but we are not concerned with who was to blame for the start of the war. So please don't rise to the bait and cross-examine him on that answer. We're not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I understood long ago that that was not the subject of concern to the Chamber and never mentioned it, but there is a reason I'm asking the witness about these matters. Not to prove who started what, simply challenge something that the Prosecutor asks almost all the witnesses, that is, about the armament, about their possession at the very beginning of the conflict, and you will see through my other questions that I have good reason to ask those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may well have, Mr. Bakrac, but may I also remind you of something which has been said during the course of this case as indeed in other cases. Let us assume that the Muslims were armed and that they did attack members of the Serb civilian population. That does not mean that there was not also an attack by the Serbs upon the Muslim civilian population. The two are not mutually exclusive. So we are still not terribly interested in this issue. It may be that you can make it relevant in some way, but it is not a matter which on the face of it seems to be helping us very much. All right. We'll adjourn now, and I remind you we will be sitting at 10.00 tomorrow and sitting only for the morning. We will be sitting from 10.00 to 11.30 and then from 12.00 until 1.30. So we adjourn now until 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of February, 2001, at 10.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.02 p.m.,
